name: Jet engine
title: Turbofan jet engine
intro: This is an airliner's cutaway turbofan engine, showing the fan, compressors, combustor and turbines. Ask me "Where does the thrust come from?"
suggest: Where does the thrust come from?
How does a plane slow down after landing?
looksLike: jet engine, aircraft engine, turbofan, turbine engine, airplane, aeroplane

nacelle_inlet.name: Inlet lip
nacelle_inlet.info: Rounded front intake lip that guides airflow smoothly into the fan even at high pitch angles or in crosswinds.

fan.name: Fan
fan.info: Large front fan. Most of the air it pushes bypasses the core and blows straight out the back, generating most of the engine's thrust.

fan_case.name: Fan case
fan_case.info: Heavy containment ring around the fan designed to trap a blade if one ever breaks off.

fan_cowl_left.name: Left fan cowl
fan_cowl_left.info: Left outer cowling door that swings up so mechanics can service external accessories.

fan_cowl_right.name: Right fan cowl
fan_cowl_right.info: Right outer cowling door that swings open for maintenance.

thrust_reverser.name: Thrust reverser
thrust_reverser.info: Slides aft after touchdown to block bypass air and redirect it forward through cascade vanes, helping brake the aircraft.

booster.name: Low-pressure compressor
booster.info: Mounted right behind the fan on the low-pressure shaft to give core air its first stage of compression.

hp_compressor.name: High-pressure compressor
hp_compressor.info: Multiple rows of progressively smaller blades that squeeze core air to dozens of times atmospheric pressure.

combustor.name: Combustor
combustor.info: Sprays fuel into the compressed air for continuous combustion, heating gas past a thousand degrees so it expands rapidly.

hp_turbine.name: High-pressure turbine
hp_turbine.info: Spun by the hottest gas leaving the combustor to drive the high-pressure compressor via the high-pressure shaft.

lp_turbine.name: Low-pressure turbine
lp_turbine.info: Larger rear turbine stages that extract remaining gas energy to spin the front fan and booster via the low-pressure shaft.

hp_shaft.name: High-pressure shaft
hp_shaft.info: Hollow outer shaft linking the high-pressure turbine to the high-pressure compressor; spins at the highest rpm.

lp_shaft.name: Low-pressure shaft
lp_shaft.info: Long inner shaft running through the hollow high-pressure shaft from the rear low-pressure turbine to the front fan.

core_case.name: Core case
core_case.info: High-strength casing enclosing the core compressors, combustor and turbines.

core_cowl.name: Core cowl
core_cowl.info: Streamlined fairing around the engine core that forms the inner wall of the bypass duct.

exhaust.name: Exhaust nozzle
exhaust.info: Rear nozzle that accelerates hot core exhaust gas to add thrust.

radial_driveshaft.name: Radial driveshaft
radial_driveshaft.info: Bevel-gear shaft (48:32) tapping power from the high-pressure shaft to run the accessory gearbox—or cranking the core during engine start.

accessory_gearbox.name: Accessory gearbox
accessory_gearbox.info: Bottom-mounted gearbox driving the electrical generators, fuel pumps and hydraulic pumps for the aircraft.

stand.name: Stand
stand.info: Ground display cradle supporting the engine; not part of the aircraft.

steps.say: The front fan pushes a huge volume of air; most of it skips the core and blows straight through the outer bypass duct.

quiz.q: Where does most of an airliner turbofan's thrust come from?
options: The outer bypass air pushed by the fan
Moving a large mass of bypass air at moderate speed produces about 80% of the thrust while saving fuel and reducing noise.
Flames shooting out the tailpipe
Core exhaust provides only a small part of the thrust; most of its energy is spent spinning the turbines.
Explosions inside the combustor
Combustion is a steady continuous burn whose energy primarily drives the turbines and fan.

steps.say: Air entering the inner core is squeezed stage by stage by the low-pressure and high-pressure compressors.

quiz.q: Why must the air be tightly compressed before fuel is burned?
options: Compressed air expands much more powerfully when heated, boosting efficiency
Higher pressure before combustion yields far greater expansion work to spin the turbines.
To cool the air down
Compressing a gas actually raises its temperature significantly.
To make the engine lighter
Multi-stage compressors add weight, but are essential for thermal efficiency.

steps.say: Fuel burns continuously in the compressed air, making the gas extremely hot so it expands rapidly rearward.
Expanding gas spins the high- and low-pressure turbines, which drive the front compressors and fan via twin shafts before exiting the nozzle.

quiz.q: What drives the huge fan at the very front of the engine?
options: The low-pressure turbine at the back, via the long low-pressure shaft
The inner low-pressure shaft runs all the way from the rear turbine through the centre of the engine to the front fan.
An electric motor
The engine's own gas turbine powers the fan mechanically without electric motors.
Oncoming wind from the plane's motion
Windmilling only creates drag; the turbine must actively spin the fan to produce thrust.

spools.title: Two shafts, each at its own speed

steps.say: The inner low-pressure shaft links the front fan, booster and rear low-pressure turbine, spinning at a lower rpm.
The hollow outer high-pressure shaft links the high-pressure compressor and turbine, spinning several times faster around the inner shaft.

quiz.q: Why not mount the fan and the high-pressure compressor on a single shaft at the same speed?
options: The big fan would go supersonic at the high rpm needed by the small compressor
Large fan tips exceed the speed of sound if spun too fast, while small compressor blades need high rpm; twin shafts let each run at its ideal speed.
To make manufacturing simpler
Nested coaxial shafts are much harder to build, but dramatically improve engine efficiency.
One shaft is just a backup
Both shafts run simultaneously to handle low-pressure and high-pressure stages separately.

steps.say: A radial driveshaft taps power from the high-pressure shaft via bevel gears to run the accessory gearbox below.

service.title: Opening it up, and reverse thrust on landing

steps.say: Swinging open the left and right fan cowls gives mechanics access to the accessory gearbox and plumbing.
After landing, the thrust reverser slides back, blocking bypass air and deflecting it forward to help slow the plane.

quiz.q: When the thrust reverser is deployed after landing, does the engine fan spin backward?
options: No, the fan keeps spinning the same way while doors redirect the airflow forward
Turbines cannot reverse rotation; blocker doors and vanes deflect the bypass air forward instead.
Yes, the fan spins in reverse
Jet engine blades are angled to spin in one direction only.
The engine shuts off completely
Pilots actually rev the engine up during reverse thrust to blow more air forward.

hp_shaft.title: Broken high-pressure shaft
hp_shaft.short: The turbines turn, but the compressor has stopped
hp_shaft.symptom: The front fan and rear turbines are spinning, but the high-pressure compressor in the middle has stopped and thrust has plunged. What's broken?
hp_shaft.hint: The high-pressure compressor is driven by the high-pressure turbine. Check the outer hollow shaft running between them through the centre of the combustor.
hp_shaft.observe: Look at the spinning high-pressure turbine behind the combustor, then look at the stopped high-pressure compressor ahead of it: what connects them?
whys: A flameout would starve the rear turbines of hot gas, yet you can see both turbines spinning at the back.
Look at the front—the fan is spinning fine on the inner low-pressure shaft. The stopped part is the high-pressure compressor inside the core.
hp_shaft.cause: The high-pressure shaft snapped, so the spinning high-pressure turbine can no longer drive the high-pressure compressor.
hp_shaft.why: Why does engine thrust drop sharply when the high-pressure shaft breaks and stops the high-pressure compressor?
hp_shaft.answer: The high-pressure shaft carries turbine power to the high-pressure compressor to squeeze air into the combustor. When it breaks, air isn't compressed, combustion weakens, and thrust drops.
reasons: The high-pressure shaft is a fuel pipe, so breaking it cuts off fuel to the combustor.
The high-pressure shaft bolts the engine to the wing, so breaking it disconnects the thrust.
